c.tagline: Aragón's grand riverside capital of basilicas, Mudéjar towers, and legendary tapas.

taxi.fareNote: Uber operates only on a limited basis; Cabify and traditional metered white taxis are the reliable options.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Watch pockets in the crowded El Tubo tapas alleys and especially amid Fiestas del Pilar crowds.

hood_desc: The monumental heart around Plaza del Pilar, the Basílica del Pilar, La Seo cathedral and Roman-era ruins; best for first-timers who want the landmarks and tapas at their doorstep.
A warren of narrow lanes packed with historic tapas bars and bodegas just off Plaza del Pilar; the go-to for eating and drinking your way through Zaragoza after dark.
The commercial spine along Paseo de la Independencia, full of department stores, cafes and belle-époque facades; a convenient, well-connected base steps from the old town and the tram.
A practical, modern residential district built around the AVE high-speed station and intermodal bus terminal; handy for early trains and budget hotels, a short tram ride from the center.
A leafy contemporary district across the Ebro built up around the Expo 2008 grounds and the Water Park; calm, spacious and family-friendly, linked to downtown by the tram.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though some prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: The tram runs roughly 5:45 AM to 11:00 PM (later on weekends); daytime city buses run about 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM, with a limited night-bus (búho) network on weekend nights.
transit.note: Zaragoza has no metro; a single modern tram line (Line 1) runs north-south through the center, complemented by an extensive city bus network and one Cercanías commuter-rail line (C-1).
transit.pay: Pay contactless with a bank card or the rechargeable Tarjeta Ciudadana/Lazcard; single rides are about €1.35-1.40 and can also be bought from tram machines. Cash is accepted on buses.

train: Zaragoza-Delicias (AVE high-speed to Madrid & Barcelona, plus Renfe long-distance)

transit.m: Airport bus (line 501) to Paseo María Agustín / city center (~35 min)

tip.r: Service is included; locals typically round up or leave small change, or 5-10% for good restaurant service.

food.name: Ternasco de Aragon
food.desc: Aragon's protected milk-fed lamb, slow-roasted with potatoes and rosemary until the skin crackles and the meat slides off the bone.

places.name: Casa Lac
places.note: Licensed as a restaurant in 1825; classic wood-panelled dining room doing textbook roast ternasco.

places.name: La Rinconada de Lorenzo
places.note: Old-guard Aragonese house famous for its wood-oven lamb and regional cooking.

places.name: Palomeque
places.note: Modern take on Aragonese classics; reliable lamb and stews near Plaza del Pilar.

food.name: Migas a la pastora
food.desc: Shepherds' fried breadcrumbs cooked with garlic, chorizo and bacon, often crowned with grapes or a fried egg. Aragon's great peasant dish.

places.name: La Migueria
places.note: Specialist house serving more than thirty versions of migas, from classic to creative.

places.name: Palomeque
places.note: Known for migas with foie and wild mushrooms alongside the traditional version.

places.name: La Rinconada de Lorenzo
places.note: Long-running Aragonese kitchen where migas come as a proper sit-down plate.

food.name: Borrajas con patata
food.desc: Borage, the fuzzy green stalk Aragon is obsessed with, boiled with potato and dressed with olive oil and garlic. Sweet, faintly cucumber-like.

places.name: La Rinconada de Lorenzo
places.note: Puts borrajas on the menu year-round, the way locals actually eat them.

places.name: Casa Lac
places.note: Historic house that treats humble Aragonese vegetables with real respect.

places.name: Mercado Central de Zaragoza
places.note: Modernista market hall; buy borrajas at source and see how central they are here.

food.name: Bacalao al ajoarriero
food.desc: Salt cod shredded and stewed with garlic, peppers and tomato into a rich, rust-coloured mash. An inland classic in a landlocked region.

places.name: Casa Lac
places.note: Traditional recipe done in one of Spain's oldest continuously licensed restaurants.

places.name: Lamaribel Escabechado
places.note: Tiny corner bar in El Tubo known for cured, pickled and preserved specialities.

places.name: Bodegas Almau
places.note: Century-old wine bar with excellent salt-cod and anchovy tapas.

food.name: Champinones y tapas de El Tubo
food.desc: Grilled mushroom caps stacked with garlic and prawn on a cocktail stick, plus banderillas, eaten standing up bar to bar for a couple of euros a plate.

places.name: El Champi
places.note: The mushroom bar locals name first; one dish, done perfectly, all night.

places.name: Bodegas Almau
places.note: Historic bodega famous for anchovies and vermouth to go with them.

places.name: El Meli del Tubo
places.note: Creative Aragonese tapas in a lively modern room in the heart of the tapas maze.

food.name: Frutas de Aragon
food.desc: Candied local fruit, peach, pear, plum, dipped in dark chocolate. Zaragoza's signature sweet, sold in ribboned boxes for over a century.

places.name: Pasteleria Fantoba
places.area: Calle Don Jaime I, Casco Antiguo
places.note: Confectioner since 1856; the reference address for frutas de Aragon.

places.name: Mercado Central de Zaragoza
places.note: Several stalls sell boxed frutas de Aragon and other regional sweets.

places.name: Pasteleria Ascaso
places.note: Well-regarded local chain for frutas de Aragon and trenza-style pastries.

food.name: Vino de Carinena or Campo de Borja
food.desc: Aragon's old-vine garnacha reds, dark and generous, from two DOs an hour outside the city. Ordered by the glass everywhere in El Tubo.

places.name: Bodegas Almau
places.note: Classic bodega pouring Aragonese wine by the glass since 1870.

places.name: El Meli del Tubo
places.note: Good regional list to pair with the tapas crawl.

places.name: Casa Lac
places.note: Deep Aragonese cellar in a historic dining room.

food.name: Vermut de grifo
food.desc: Draught vermouth poured over ice with an olive and orange, the standard Sunday-before-lunch ritual across the old town.

places.name: Bodegas Almau
places.note: Vermouth on tap with anchovy tapas; the archetypal Zaragoza vermut stop.

places.name: El Tubo bars, Calle Libertad and Calle Estebanes
places.note: Almost every bar on these two lanes runs a vermouth tap at midday.

places.name: Casa Lac
places.note: Aperitivo hour in the ground-floor bar of the historic building.

landmarks: Basílica del Pilar
A colossal multi-domed basilica on the Ebro honoring the Virgin of the Pillar, with Goya frescoes and a tower lift for river views.
La Seo (Cathedral of the Savior)
Zaragoza's other cathedral layers Romanesque, Gothic and Baroque styles; its UNESCO-listed Mudéjar wall and tapestry museum are unmissable.
Aljafería Palace
An 11th-century Moorish pleasure palace of intricate stucco arcades, later home to Aragon's kings and today the regional parliament.
Plaza del Pilar
One of Europe's largest pedestrian squares, sweeping past the basilica, monumental fountains and Goya statues toward La Seo.
Puente de Piedra
The 15th-century 'Bridge of Lions' spans the Ebro, delivering the classic sunset reflection view of the Pilar's clustered domes.
Caesaraugusta Roman Route
Four linked museums trace Roman Zaragoza—forum, river port, baths and a 6,000-seat theatre—hidden beneath the modern city's streets.
Goya Museum
A Renaissance palace devoted to Zaragoza's most famous son, Francisco de Goya, including his complete engraving series.
Mercado Central
A splendidly restored 1903 iron-and-glass market hall piled with Aragonese produce, standing beside remnants of the Roman walls.
El Tubo
A knot of narrow lanes where locals hop between crowded tapas bars—Zaragoza's essential eating and nightlife experience.
Expo 2008 Riverfront
The Ebro banks flaunt Zaha Hadid's Bridge Pavilion and the 76-meter Water Tower, futuristic legacies of the 2008 world exposition.

train.note: No international trains. Zaragoza-Delicias is a major junction on the Madrid-Barcelona high-speed line, with AVE services reaching either city in about 1h20-1h30, plus Ouigo and Iryo low-cost high-speed operators on the same route. The Canfranc line north toward the French border carries only regional trains and stops short of a through connection to France. Booking opens around 60 days ahead.

bus.note: Coaches use the terminal built into Delicias station, so bus and train share one building. ALSA and Avanza run frequently to Madrid, Barcelona, Pamplona and Huesca; the train is faster on the Madrid and Barcelona corridors but the bus is cheaper.

ferry.note: Zaragoza is deep inland in the Ebro valley with no navigable passenger route, so there are no ferries. Sightseeing boats run short trips on the Ebro through the city.

half.name: Monasterio de Piedra
half.blurb: 12th-century monastery set in a park of waterfalls, caves, and a lake carved by the Piedra River.

half.name: Tarazona
half.blurb: Hillside town with a Mudéjar cathedral and a bullring converted into a circular residential plaza.

half.name: Belchite
half.blurb: Ruined town left destroyed since the Spanish Civil War, preserved as a shell of bombed-out buildings.
